analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurance to cover mammograms, Pap tests, and colon and prostate cancer screening.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in October 2003, sent to four House committees and three subcommittees, and never received a vote before the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required group and individual health insurance to cover key cancer screenings at set intervals: annual mammograms for women 40 and over (or younger women at high risk), clinical breast exams, Pap tests and pelvic exams, colorectal screening for people 50 and over, and prostate screening for men 50 and over or at high risk, including Black men and men with a family history. It would also have barred insurers from dodging the requirement by denying enrollment and required plans to disclose benefit and provider information to patients. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People with job-based or individual health insurance — especially women 40 and over, adults 50 and over, and people with a family history of breast, colon, or prostate cancer — who would gain guaranteed coverage for early-detection screening without insurers excluding them to avoid the cost.

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans and insurers to cover annual mammograms for women 40 and over (and high-risk younger women), clinical breast exams, annual Pap tests and pelvic exams for women 18 and over, colorectal cancer screening for adults 50 and over, and prostate screening for men 50 and over or at high risk, including African American men and men with a first-degree family history [S2] [S3].

Bars insurers from denying enrollment or renewal solely to avoid the screening mandate, and bars plans from paying individuals to accept less coverage or penalizing providers who order the screenings [S3].
Applies the same screening coverage to individual-market insurance policies and to the Federal Employees Health Benefits program, not just employer plans [S2] [S3].
Requires plans to disclose in writing what screening benefits are covered, what cost-sharing applies, and which providers participate, annually and on request [S2] [S3].

Lets the Secretary of Health and Human Services update the covered screenings over time as medical evidence changes, on petition by individuals or organizations, without diminishing coverage [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers who sponsor group health plans bear the cost of the added claims for screening tests, which would flow through as higher premiums for policyholders and employers.

drawbacks.text: The mandate adds covered services that insurers and self-insured employers must pay for, and the bill explicitly allows plans to keep imposing deductibles and coinsurance on the screenings, so some of the added cost could still reach patients at the point of care [S3].

Requiring coverage of screening methods chosen by the treating provider, including prostate testing, could drive screening beyond what medical guidelines recommend, generating follow-up procedures and worry for patients without clear mortality benefit — a long-running criticism of broad prostate screening mandates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Guaranteed coverage of proven early-detection tests catches cancers when treatment is cheaper and more likely to work, which benefits patients and can offset costs by avoiding late-stage care. The main cost is higher premiums, and the bill's weakness is that it permits plans to keep charging deductibles and coinsurance on the very screenings it mandates, which could blunt the benefit for lower-income enrollees.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees and then three subcommittees, and none of them ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney introduced the bill in the House on October 21, 2003 [S1] [S5].

The Speaker referred it to four committees — Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, Ways and Means, and Government Reform — a multi-committee referral that splits jurisdiction and makes consideration harder [S5] [S3].
Within three weeks it was sent to three subcommittees: Health, Employer-Employee Relations, and Civil Service and Agency Organization [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the action history; the bill died at the end of the 108th Congress on January 3, 2005 [S5].
It attracted 15 cosponsors, all of them House Democrats, and no Republican cosponsors [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers avoided a new federal mandate requiring them to pay for cancer screenings, and no committee ever had to take a position on it.

for.name: Rep. Carolyn Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Cancer Screening Coverage Act of 2003 in the House.

for.name: 15 of 205 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.

against.name: House committee chairs of the 108th Congress
against.role: Chairs of Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, Ways and Means, and Government Reform
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill never left subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Democrat; the bill had no Republican cosponsors and died in committees controlled by the Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to pay for a defined set of cancer screenings in group, individual, and FEHB coverage, and to disclose benefit details, adding claims costs. A screening caught early also costs far less than late-stage cancer treatment, so the mandate reduces the worst-case claims while adding routine ones.

Self-insured employer plans would have had to cover the screenings under ERISA and the tax code, raising their health benefit costs. Some of that cost typically passes to workers as premiums or wage trade-offs.
Mandated coverage of mammography, colonoscopy, and prostate testing creates guaranteed paying demand for imaging centers, path labs, and screening clinicians.
